questions.subject: obs
questions.title: Layer excluded from the placental barrier
questions.question: The placental barrier does not include:

options.D: The endothelium of maternal blood vessels
options.E: The endothelium of fetal blood vessels

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this layer IS part of the barrier). The syncytiotrophoblast is the outer, maternal-blood-facing layer of the placental barrier.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this layer IS part of the barrier, at least in early pregnancy). The cytotrophoblast contributes to the barrier until it becomes discontinuous later in pregnancy as the barrier thins.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this layer IS part of the barrier). The primary (connective tissue) mesoderm, with the villus's fetal capillaries embedded in it, forms part of the barrier.
explanations.D: Correct. Maternal blood bathes the chorionic villi directly within the intervillous space -- it is not contained within its own maternal endothelium at the villus interface, unlike fetal blood, which stays inside fetal capillaries throughout. The placental barrier is therefore built entirely from fetal-derived tissue (trophoblast, connective tissue mesoderm, and fetal capillary endothelium); no maternal vessel wall is part of it.
explanations.E: Incorrect (i.e. this layer IS part of the barrier). The endothelium of the fetal capillaries within the villus is the innermost layer of the barrier, in contact with fetal blood.

questions.learning_objective: State that the placental barrier is built entirely from fetal tissue and does not include maternal vessel endothelium.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 1 (d, no remark)
field_notes.reuse: Overlaid onto the live CON-OBS-7C3A7E3650A747 ("Placental barrier includes syncytiotrophoblast, mesenchyme, cytotrophoblast, and fetal-capillary wall") rather than minted fresh -- same fact stated from the inclusion side.

questions.subject: obs
questions.title: Site of implantation causing placenta praevia
questions.question: Placenta praevia results from implantation of the blastocyst in the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Implantation in the pelvic peritoneum describes a form of abdominal (extrauterine) ectopic pregnancy, not placenta praevia, which is by definition an intrauterine implantation site.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The uterine tube is where tubal ectopic pregnancy occurs, not placenta praevia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Like the medial part, the lateral (ampullary) part of the uterine tube is a tubal ectopic pregnancy site, not placenta praevia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Implantation in the upper part of the uterus (the fundus or body) is the normal implantation site and does not cause placenta praevia.
explanations.E: Correct. Placenta praevia occurs when the blastocyst implants in the lower part of the uterus, so that the developing placenta lies over or near the internal cervical os. Because this places the placenta in the path the fetus must pass through at delivery, placenta praevia is a recognised cause of antepartum haemorrhage and can obstruct a vaginal delivery.

questions.learning_objective: State that placenta praevia results from implantation in the lower part of the uterus.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 2 (e/placenta praevia=implantation in lower part of [the uterus])

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Mechanism preventing polyspermy
questions.question: Prevents penetration of the oocyte by more than one sperm:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The acrosome reaction is what lets the fertilising sperm itself penetrate the corona radiata and zona pellucida; it is not the block that stops subsequent sperm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Capacitation is a prerequisite the sperm must undergo before it can fertilise at all; it plays no role in blocking additional sperm afterward.
explanations.C: Correct. Fusion of the first sperm with the oocyte membrane triggers cortical granule release, which alters the oocyte's surrounding coat. This bank's own terminology labels the resulting barrier the vitelline (membrane) block, more commonly taught as the zona reaction. Either name describes the same event: it prevents any further sperm from penetrating and fertilising the same oocyte (polyspermy).
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cervical plug is a mucus barrier at the cervix relevant to ascending infection and early pregnancy, not to blocking polyspermy at the oocyte itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The decidual reaction is the endometrial stromal-cell change that supports implantation, occurring later and at a different site than the polyspermy block.

questions.learning_objective: State that cortical-granule-triggered change to the oocyte's surrounding coat blocks polyspermy.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 3 (c/vitelline block)

questions.author_notes: This bank's key labels the polyspermy block "vitelline membrane"/"vitelline block" (option C); standard embryology teaching more often calls the same cortical-granule-triggered barrier the zona reaction. Kept the bank's own terminology per the printed key rather than silently relabelling the option.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Day implantation is completed
questions.question: Implantation of blastocyst is completed in which post-fertilization day?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Day 5 is roughly when the blastocyst forms and is still free in the uterine cavity, well before implantation begins.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Day 7 is approximately when implantation begins (the blastocyst starts to attach and the trophoblast starts to invade), not when it is completed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Day 9 falls within the implantation process but is still before it is fully completed.
explanations.D: Correct. Implantation is a process, not an instant. It begins around day 6-7, when the blastocyst attaches to and begins invading the endometrium. It is completed by about day 11-12, by which point the blastocyst is fully embedded within the endometrial stroma and the surface epithelium has closed over it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Day 13 is beyond the completion of implantation and instead falls within the events of the second week that follow it (bilaminar disc and extraembryonic mesoderm formation).

questions.learning_objective: State that implantation is completed by about the 11th day after fertilisation.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 4 (d/11th day)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Origin of the fetal part of the placenta
questions.question: The fetal part of placenta is derived from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Decidua capsularis is the maternal endometrium covering the implanted conceptus on the uterine-lumen side; it thins and eventually fuses with decidua parietalis, contributing nothing to the placenta.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Decidua basalis is maternal tissue -- it forms the maternal part of the placenta, not the fetal part this question asks about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Decidua parietalis lines the rest of the uterine cavity away from the implantation site and takes no part in the placenta at all.
explanations.D: Correct. The chorion frondosum is the region of chorion adjacent to the decidua basalis, where the chorionic villi remain well developed and continue to branch; it persists as the fetal (villous) part of the placenta. Its counterpart, the chorion laeve, is the rest of the chorion, whose villi degenerate as it is pushed away from the richly vascular decidua basalis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The chorion laeve ("smooth chorion") is the part whose villi degenerate; it does not contribute to the placenta and instead fuses with the decidua parietalis to form part of the fetal membranes.

questions.learning_objective: State that the chorion frondosum forms the fetal part of the placenta.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 5 (d/chorion frondosum)
field_notes.reuse: Overlaid onto the pending Kasr concept CON-DEV-E099FAA01BEAEB (101-ISK-mcq-concepts.md, chorionic villi types), whose own definition already states "the chorion carrying well-developed villi is the chorion frondosum, which persists as the fetal part of the placenta" -- covers this fact directly, not minted fresh.

questions.subject: obs
questions.title: Commonest site of ectopic pregnancy
questions.question: The commonest site of ectopic pregnancy is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The internal os is a landmark of the cervix/lower uterine segment relevant to placenta praevia, not a recognised site of ectopic implantation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ovarian ectopic pregnancy occurs, but it is a rare form, not the commonest.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Abdominal/peritoneal ectopic pregnancy occurs, but it is rare, typically secondary to a failed tubal pregnancy, not the commonest primary site.
explanations.D: Correct. The fertilised oocyte normally spends its first several days travelling along the uterine tube before the resulting blastocyst reaches the uterine cavity. If that journey stalls or the blastocyst implants prematurely, it does so within the tube itself, most often in its ampullary part. This makes the uterine tube by far the commonest site of ectopic implantation, accounting for the great majority of ectopic pregnancies.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cervical ectopic pregnancy occurs, but it is one of the rarest forms, not the commonest.

questions.learning_objective: State that the uterine tube is the commonest site of ectopic pregnancy.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 6 (d/uterine tubes)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Fate of the blastocoele
questions.question: The blastocoele becomes the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The amniotic sac develops from a separate cavity that appears within the inner cell mass (between the epiblast and the overlying cytotrophoblast), not from the blastocoele.
explanations.B: Correct. The blastocoele is the fluid-filled cavity of the blastocyst. The hypoblast cells that line it spread to form the exocoelomic (Heuser's) membrane, and together with the hypoblast this lining converts the blastocoele into the primary yolk sac (later remodelled into the smaller secondary/definitive yolk sac).
explanations.C: Incorrect. The extraembryonic coelom (chorionic cavity) forms later, within the extraembryonic mesoderm, splitting it into somatic and splanchnic layers -- it is a separate, later cavity, not a direct continuation of the blastocoele.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The intraembryonic coelom forms later still, within the lateral plate mesoderm of the embryonic disc itself, unrelated to the blastocoele.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The chorionic cavity is the same structure as the extraembryonic coelom, formed later within the extraembryonic mesoderm rather than being the blastocoele itself.

questions.topic: Embryology - Events of the second week
questions.learning_objective: State that the blastocoele becomes the (primary) yolk sac.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 7 (b/the blastocoele forms the yolk sac)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Composition of the chorionic vesicle wall
questions.question: The wall of chorionic vesicle is made of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast together make up the trophoblast alone, without the mesodermal layer that lines it once the extraembryonic mesoderm forms -- this describes an earlier stage (the wall of the blastocyst/early implanted conceptus), not the definitive chorionic vesicle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The exocoelomic membrane lines the primary yolk sac, not the chorion, and is not part of the chorionic wall.
explanations.C: Incorrect. As in option B, the exocoelomic membrane belongs to the yolk sac lining, not the chorionic vesicle wall, and syncytiotrophoblast alone omits the cytotrophoblast layer.
explanations.D: Correct. Once extraembryonic mesoderm forms, it lines the inside of the trophoblast. The chorion -- the definitive wall of the chorionic vesicle -- therefore consists of the trophoblast (cytotrophoblast + syncytiotrophoblast) plus this extraembryonic somatic mesoderm. This is the same somatic mesodermal layer that also lines the amnion, as distinct from the splanchnic layer that covers the yolk sac.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The extraembryonic splanchnic mesoderm covers the yolk sac, not the chorion; the chorion's mesodermal component is specifically the somatic layer.

questions.topic: Embryology - Events of the second week
questions.learning_objective: State that the chorionic vesicle wall is made of trophoblast plus extraembryonic somatic mesoderm.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 8 (d/trophoblast + extraembryonic mesoderm)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Identity of the cell fertilised by the sperm
questions.question: The cell that is fertilized by the sperm is the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The primary oocyte has already completed its first meiotic division, becoming a secondary oocyte, by the time it is ovulated and available for fertilisation.
explanations.B: Correct. The cell released at ovulation and penetrated by the sperm is the secondary oocyte, still arrested at metaphase of the second meiotic division. Sperm entry provides the calcium signal that triggers completion of this second division, after which the cell is properly called a mature (fertilised) ovum.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A "mature ovum" only exists once the second meiotic division has completed -- that is, only after fertilisation has already begun, not the cell fertilisation acts upon at the outset.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The first polar body is a discarded product of the first meiotic division; it is not a gamete and cannot be fertilised.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The second polar body is likewise a discarded, non-fertilisable by-product, extruded from the secondary oocyte only once the second meiotic division completes at fertilisation.

questions.learning_objective: State that the secondary oocyte, not the mature ovum, is the cell fertilised by the sperm.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 9 (b/2ry oocyte)

questions.subject: obs
questions.title: Term for implantation in the lower uterine segment
questions.question: Implantation in the lower uterine segment is called placenta .....:

explanations.A: Correct. Placenta praevia (previa) is the term for a placenta that has developed from a blastocyst implanted in the lower uterine segment, so that it lies over or near the internal cervical os. It is defined by abnormal implantation site, in contrast to the other named placental anomalies below, which describe abnormal attachment depth or shape rather than site.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Placenta accreta describes abnormally deep attachment of the placenta into the myometrium (with little or no intervening decidua), a depth-of-invasion abnormality, not a site abnormality.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Placenta membranacea describes a placenta that remains abnormally thin and spread over most of the chorionic sac, a shape abnormality, not specifically a lower-segment site abnormality.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Placenta succenturiata describes an accessory placental lobe connected to the main placenta by vessels, a shape/number abnormality, not a lower-segment site abnormality.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Placenta percreta describes the most severe degree of abnormal attachment, in which villi penetrate through the full thickness of the myometrium and beyond, a depth-of-invasion abnormality, not specifically a site one.

questions.learning_objective: Name placenta praevia as the term for implantation in the lower uterine segment.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 10 (a/placenta praevia)

questions.subject: obs
questions.title: Part of the decidua the chorion leave faces
questions.question: The chorion leave faces which part of the decidua?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Decidua basalis is faced by the chorion frondosum, not the chorion leave -- that pairing forms the placenta proper, the opposite of this question's regressed-membrane pairing.
explanations.B: Correct. As the gestational sac expands, the chorion away from the implantation site loses its villi and becomes the smooth chorion leave (laeve). This regressed chorion directly faces the decidua capsularis, the thin layer of endometrium stretched over the conceptus on the side away from the myometrium. The chorion frondosum, by contrast, faces the decidua basalis, forming the placenta proper.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Parietalis" is not a printed option in this stem, and decidua parietalis (lining the rest of the uterine cavity away from the implantation site) is not faced by the chorion leave either -- it does not overlie the gestational sac at all.
explanations.D: "Lateralis" is not a standard decidua region; no such term applies to the chorion-decidua relationship being tested here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Frondosum is the fetal part of the placenta, faced by the decidua basalis -- it is the chorion frondosum/decidua basalis pairing, not the chorion leave, that this option describes.

questions.learning_objective: State that the chorion leave faces the decidua capsularis.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 11 = b (Decidua capsularis)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure preventing enlargement of the cleaving zygote
questions.question: Enlargement of the cleaving zygote is prevented by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The corona radiata is the granulosa-cell layer the sperm must penetrate to fertilise the oocyte; it is shed before cleavage and plays no role in confining the dividing zygote's size.
explanations.B: Correct. As the zygote cleaves, each division produces more, smaller blastomeres, but the intact zona pellucida is an unyielding acellular coat that confines the whole conceptus within a fixed outer size. Growth is achieved by dividing into more, smaller cells, not by the conceptus getting physically bigger. The zona persists in this role until it is later shed at hatching, just before implantation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The vitelline (oocyte) membrane lies inside the zona pellucida and is the site of sperm-oocyte fusion; it is not the structure that constrains the cleaving zygote's overall size.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The Fallopian (uterine) tube is the conduit that transports the cleaving conceptus toward the uterus; its diameter does not confine the zygote's size the way the zona pellucida does.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Follicular (granulosa) cells form the corona radiata around the oocyte before fertilisation and are shed early -- they are not present to constrain the zygote during cleavage.

questions.learning_objective: State that the zona pellucida prevents the cleaving zygote from enlarging.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 12 = b (Zona pellucida)

questions.subject: obs
questions.title: Tissues the placenta is derived from
questions.question: The placenta is derived from the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chorion frondosum is correctly the fetal contributor, but decidua capsularis is instead faced by the chorion leave, not paired with the frondosum -- the capsularis regresses along with the leave rather than forming the placenta.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Both terms here are the regressed-membrane pair (chorion leave / decidua capsularis), not the placenta-forming pair.
explanations.C: Correct. The definitive placenta has a fetal part and a maternal part. Its fetal part is the chorion frondosum, the villous region of chorion derived from the embryo. Its maternal part is the decidua basalis, the endometrium underlying the implantation site, and together these two structures constitute the placenta.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chorion leave and decidua parietalis are both non-placental structures -- the leave regresses and fuses with the parietalis later in pregnancy, obliterating the uterine cavity, but neither forms the placenta.
explanations.E: Incorrect. This option pairs two chorionic regions together and omits any decidual (maternal) contribution -- the placenta needs both a fetal (chorionic) and a maternal (decidual) part.

questions.learning_objective: State that the placenta is derived from the chorion frondosum and decidua basalis.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 13 = c (confirmed by re-OCR at 400/600 dpi after an initial pass misread the letter as e; the remark text "Chorion frondosum + decidua basalis" matches option c exactly)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Composition of a secondary chorionic villus
questions.question: A 2ry chorionic villus is made of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cytotrophoblast plus syncytiotrophoblast, with no mesenchymal core, describes a primary villus -- the stage before mesoderm has invaded, not the secondary stage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mesoderm that invades to form a secondary villus is the primary (1ry, extraembryonic) mesoderm, not a "2ry mesoderm" -- "secondary" describes the villus's own maturation stage, not a second generation of mesoderm.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Adding fetal capillaries describes the tertiary (vascularised) villus, one stage further matured than the secondary villus this question asks about.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This combination omits the cytotrophoblast and, like option C, wrongly adds fetal capillaries -- neither belongs to the secondary-villus stage.
explanations.E: Correct. Once extraembryonic (primary) mesoderm invades the trophoblastic core of a primary villus, the villus becomes a secondary villus. Its composition is then trophoblast (cytotrophoblast plus syncytiotrophoblast) plus this primary mesoderm core. It does not yet carry fetal blood vessels -- that step, vascularisation, is what defines the next, tertiary, stage.

questions.learning_objective: State that a secondary chorionic villus consists of trophoblast plus primary mesoderm.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 14 = e (confirmed by re-OCR at 400/600 dpi; remark "Trophoblast + 1ry mesoderm" matches option e)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure preventing enlargement of the dividing zygote (reworded)
questions.question: Prevents enlargement of the dividing zygote:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The vitelline (oocyte) membrane is the site of sperm-oocyte fusion, internal to the zona pellucida -- it is not the structure that confines the whole conceptus's outer size during cleavage.
explanations.B: Correct. The zona pellucida, unchanged through cleavage, keeps the overall diameter of the dividing conceptus essentially constant from the zygote through the morula. Each division adds more, smaller cells rather than making the whole conceptus bigger. This is the same size-confining function tested from a different stem wording elsewhere in this bank.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Fallopian tube's diameter is a fixed anatomical passage, not a structure that actively constrains the zygote's growth; the zona pellucida performs that role, independent of the tube's own dimensions.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gonadotrophins are pituitary/placental hormones regulating ovarian and pregnancy physiology; they play no role in physically confining the size of the cleaving zygote.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The decidual reaction is an endometrial stromal change supporting implantation, occurring later and at a different site than cleavage, so it has no bearing on the zygote's size during division.

questions.learning_objective: State that the zona pellucida prevents the dividing zygote from enlarging.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 15 = b (Zona pellucida); same fact as embryo2-q12, distinct distractor set

questions.subject: obs
questions.title: Origin of the fetal part of the placenta (2nd asking)
questions.question: The fetal part of placenta is derived from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Decidua basalis is the maternal part of the placenta, not the fetal part -- it derives from maternal endometrium, not embryonic tissue.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Decidua capsularis is a maternal structure that regresses along with the chorion leave; it does not form the fetal part of the placenta.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Decidua parietalis lines the uterine cavity away from the implantation site and is maternal in origin -- irrelevant to the fetal part of the placenta.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The chorion leave is the regressed, villus-poor chorion that faces the decidua capsularis; it does not contribute to the definitive placenta.
explanations.E: Correct. The chorion frondosum is the region of chorion bearing well-developed, branching villi. It is derived from the embryo -- built from trophoblast plus extraembryonic mesoderm -- and it constitutes the fetal part of the placenta, pairing with the maternal decidua basalis to form the definitive placenta.

questions.learning_objective: State that the fetal part of the placenta is derived from the chorion frondosum.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 16 = e (Chorion frondosum)

questions.subject: obs
questions.title: Term for cord attachment to the placental margin
questions.question: Attachment of the umbilical cord to the margin of placenta is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Placenta membranacea is an abnormally thin, diffuse placenta covering most of the uterine wall -- a shape abnormality, unrelated to where the cord attaches.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Placenta praevia marginalis describes an abnormally low implantation site (the placental edge reaching the internal os), not the site of cord insertion into the placenta.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Placenta succenturiata describes an accessory placental lobule separate from the main placental mass -- a number abnormality, not a cord-insertion term.
explanations.D: Correct. When the umbilical cord inserts at the margin (edge) of the placental disc, rather than centrally or paracentrally, this is called battledore placenta. The name comes from its resemblance to a battledore (paddle) racket, with the handle (cord) attached at the rim. It is generally a benign variant, though it carries a modestly increased risk of fetal growth restriction and cord compression.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Velamentous insertion is a more extreme abnormality in which the cord inserts into the membranes beyond the placental edge, with the vessels running unprotected through the membranes before reaching the disc -- not simply reaching the margin of the disc itself.

questions.learning_objective: Name battledore placenta as marginal attachment of the umbilical cord.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 17 = d (Battledore placenta); stem and options confirmed by direct render (page 4) after heavy OCR scrambling on this page

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Site of sperm capacitation
questions.question: The process of sperm capacitation takes place within the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sperm leave the testes not yet capacitated -- capacitation only begins once the sperm are within the female reproductive tract, not in the testes themselves.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The male urethra is a transit passage during ejaculation; capacitation requires exposure to female-tract secretions, which the sperm has not yet encountered while in the urethra.
explanations.C: Correct. In the female genital tract, the sperm undergoes capacitation: the removal of the glycoprotein coat and seminal plasma proteins from the plasma membrane overlying the acrosomal region. This change is a prerequisite for the acrosome reaction. Without it, the sperm cannot fertilise the oocyte at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ovum (oocyte) is the cell the capacitated sperm goes on to fertilise -- capacitation is a change undergone by the sperm itself, within the tract, not "within" the ovum.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The embryo exists only after fertilisation has already occurred, which itself requires prior capacitation -- capacitation cannot occur within a structure that does not yet exist.

questions.learning_objective: State that sperm capacitation takes place within the female genital tract.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.13 row 18 -- OCR recovered the remark text "Female genital tract" (matching option c exactly) across two re-OCR passes at 400/600 dpi despite a noisy letter column; corroborated by the identical fact keyed cleanly at rows 28 and 33 on the p.14 render (both = female genital tract)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Term for a villus invaded by mesoderm
questions.question: When the chorionic villus becomes invaded by mesoderm, it is called:

explanations.A: Correct. A primary villus (trophoblast only) becomes a secondary villus once extraembryonic (primary) mesoderm invades its trophoblastic core. Mesoderm invasion is exactly the event that defines this transition. Vascularisation, a separate later step, is what then advances the villus to the tertiary stage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Tertiary" describes the next stage, marked by vascularisation (fetal capillary development within the mesodermal core), not by mesoderm invasion itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Branching villus" describes the shape/arrangement of mature (typically tertiary) villi extending into the intervillous space, not the mesoderm-invasion event.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A stem (anchoring) villus is a tertiary villus that reaches and fixes to the decidua basalis -- a functional/positional label applied once the villus is already mature, not the term for newly mesoderm-invaded villi.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Anchoring villus" is synonymous with stem villus (a mature, decidua-attached tertiary villus), not the term for the earlier mesoderm-invasion event.

questions.learning_objective: Name a mesoderm-invaded villus a secondary villus.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.14 row 20 = a; stem confirmed by direct render (page 4)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Site of sperm capacitation among male-tract options
questions.question: Sperm capacitation occurs in the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The seminiferous tubules are where spermatogenesis (sperm production), not capacitation, takes place -- capacitation requires the female-tract environment, encountered only after ejaculation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The rete testis is part of the sperm's exit pathway from the testis, still within the male tract, where capacitation has not yet begun.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The epididymis is where sperm complete maturation and gain motility potential and are stored, but capacitation itself only occurs once the sperm is within the female genital tract.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The vas deferens transports sperm during ejaculation, still on the male side of the process -- capacitation has not yet occurred at this point.
explanations.E: Correct. Of the five listed structures, only the uterus is part of the female genital tract. It is within the female tract, uterus included, that sperm capacitation actually takes place. None of the male-tract structures listed here support capacitation at all.

questions.learning_objective: State that capacitation occurs in the female tract (uterus), not in any part of the male tract.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.14 row 21 = e (Uterus)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Term for a vascularized chorionic villus
questions.question: When the chorionic villus becomes vascularized, it is given the term:

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Branching villus" describes shape/arrangement, not the vascularisation event itself -- a villus can be described as branching without that word specifying whether fetal vessels are present.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Stem villus" is a positional/functional label for a mature villus anchored to the decidua basalis; vascularisation is what makes a villus tertiary, and stem villi are typically tertiary, but the term tested here specifically names the vascularisation event.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Anchoring villus" is synonymous with stem villus, describing attachment to the decidua, not the vascularisation event.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A secondary villus has a mesenchymal core but is not yet vascularised -- vascularisation is precisely the step that moves it beyond the secondary stage.
explanations.E: Correct. Once fetal blood vessels develop within the mesodermal core of a secondary villus, it becomes a tertiary (definitive) villus. Vascularisation is the defining event of this final maturation stage. A vascularised, decidua-anchored tertiary villus is also known as a stem or anchoring villus.

questions.learning_objective: Name a vascularised villus a tertiary villus.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.14 row 22 = e (Tertiary villus)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Site of the acrosomal reaction
questions.question: The site of acrosomal reaction is:

options.E: In the seminiferous tubules of the testes

explanations.A: Incorrect. The epididymis is a maturation/storage site within the male tract, well before the sperm encounters the oocyte's coverings that trigger the acrosome reaction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The vas deferens transports sperm during ejaculation, still within the male tract -- the acrosomal enzymes have not yet been released at this stage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The vagina is only the entry point after ejaculation; the acrosome reaction is triggered specifically by contact with the zona pellucida, which the sperm has not yet reached in the vagina.
explanations.D: Correct. The acrosome reaction takes place in the Fallopian tube, at the site where the capacitated sperm meets the oocyte. It is a calcium-triggered exocytosis, releasing acrosomal enzymes (acrosin, hyaluronidase). These enzymes let the sperm penetrate the corona radiata and zona pellucida.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The seminiferous tubules are the site of spermatogenesis, occurring long before capacitation or the acrosome reaction, which both require the sperm to have already left the male tract.

questions.learning_objective: State that the acrosome reaction occurs in the Fallopian tube.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.14 row 23 = d (Fallopian tube)

questions.subject: obs
questions.title: Meaning of the term battledore placenta
questions.question: The term battledore placenta means:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A divided placenta (bilobed/bipartite) is a shape abnormality of the placental disc itself, unrelated to where the cord inserts.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A placenta covering the internal os describes placenta praevia, an implantation-site abnormality, not a cord-insertion pattern.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cord attachment to the membranes beyond the placental edge (with unprotected vessels) describes velamentous insertion, a more extreme abnormality than battledore placenta.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An accessory placental lobule describes placenta succenturiata, a number abnormality, not a cord-insertion pattern.
explanations.E: Correct. Battledore placenta is defined by the umbilical cord attaching at the periphery (margin) of the placental disc, rather than centrally. This is the same fact tested from a definitional angle here, complementing the naming question tested elsewhere in this bank. The cord vessels still branch normally across the fetal surface once inserted, distinguishing this from velamentous insertion.

questions.learning_objective: Define battledore placenta as cord attachment to the placental periphery.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.14 row 24 = e (Umbilical cord attached to placenta periphery)

questions.subject: obs
questions.title: Meaning of pygopagus
questions.question: Pyopagus means:

options.A: Monozygotic twins fused at the thoracic region
options.B: Dizygotic twins fused at the thoracic region
options.C: Monozygotic twins fused at the sacral region
options.D: Dizygotic twins fused at the sacral region
options.E: Monozygotic twins fused at the head region

explanations.A: Incorrect. Thoracic-region fusion is named thoracopagus, not pygopagus -- the site named here does not match pygopagus's sacral fusion site.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Conjoined twinning is always a monozygotic phenomenon (from a single, incompletely-separated zygote); dizygotic (two-zygote) twins are never conjoined, so this option is doubly wrong.
explanations.C: Correct. Pygopagus names conjoined twins joined at the sacral (buttock) region. Since conjoined twinning always arises from incomplete separation of a single zygote, these twins are necessarily monozygotic. This is one of several named conjoined-twin patterns classified by fusion site, alongside thoracopagus and craniopagus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. As in option B, conjoined (fused) twins cannot be dizygotic; the fusion site named (sacral) is correct for pygopagus, but the zygosity is wrong.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Head-region fusion is named craniopagus, not pygopagus -- again the wrong fusion site for this term.

questions.learning_objective: Define pygopagus as monozygotic twins conjoined at the sacral region.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.14 row 25 = c

questions.subject: obs
questions.title: Placental barrier layers that disappear in late pregnancy
questions.question: The following layers of placental barrier disappear in the second half of pregnancy:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The syncytiotrophoblast is the layer that persists throughout pregnancy, directly bathed by maternal blood -- it is the cytotrophoblast, paired with the primary mesoderm, that regresses, not the syncytiotrophoblast.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fetal endothelium is a permanent, functionally essential layer of the barrier that persists throughout pregnancy -- it does not disappear alongside the primary mesoderm.
explanations.C: Correct. In the second half of pregnancy the cytotrophoblast becomes discontinuous and the primary (connective tissue) mesoderm thins markedly. These two layers therefore largely disappear from the barrier. What remains is mainly syncytiotrophoblast directly apposed to fetal capillary endothelium, a thinner barrier that shortens the diffusion distance for exchange.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The syncytiotrophoblast persists throughout pregnancy; pairing it with the regressing primary mesoderm incorrectly implies it also disappears.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Syncytiotrophoblast and fetal endothelium are exactly the two layers that remain (the barrier late in pregnancy is essentially reduced to these), not the layers that disappear.

questions.learning_objective: State that cytotrophoblast and primary mesoderm are the placental barrier layers that thin/disappear in late pregnancy.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.14 row 26 = c

questions.subject: obs
questions.title: Tissues the placenta is formed from (2nd asking)
questions.question: The placenta is formed from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Decidua basalis is correctly the maternal contributor, but the chorion leave is the regressed, non-placental chorion -- it is the chorion frondosum, not the leave, that pairs with the basalis to form the placenta.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Decidua capsularis and chorion frondosum belong to different pairings (capsularis pairs with the leave; frondosum pairs with the basalis) -- this option mismatches both.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Both decidua parietalis and chorion leave are non-placental structures; neither contributes to the definitive placenta.
explanations.D: Correct. The placenta is formed from the decidua basalis (maternal part) and the chorion frondosum (fetal part). This is the same fact tested a third time in this bank, confirming the pairing. Every other option offered here mismatches at least one of these two structures.
explanations.E: Incorrect. This option repeats "decidua capsularis" twice, omitting any chorionic contribution entirely -- the placenta requires both a decidual and a chorionic component.

questions.learning_objective: State that the placenta is formed from decidua basalis and chorion frondosum.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.14 row 27 = d

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Result of the zona (cortical) reaction
questions.question: What is the result of the zona reaction (cortical reaction)?

options.C: Sperms can now enter the egg
options.E: Sperms can no longer enter the egg

explanations.A: Incorrect. The corona radiata is a pre-existing follicular layer around the oocyte, not something newly "formed" by the zona reaction, which instead modifies the already-present zona pellucida.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The zona pellucida already exists before fertilisation; the zona reaction changes its chemical structure rather than forming it for the first time.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is the opposite of the zona reaction's effect -- the reaction blocks, rather than enables, further sperm entry.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Acrosomes are shed from individual sperm during the acrosome reaction (a separate, earlier event on the fertilising sperm itself), not removed as a result of the zona reaction on the oocyte.
explanations.E: Correct. Once the first sperm fuses with the oocyte membrane, cortical granule release triggers the zona reaction. This alters the zona pellucida's structure so that no further sperm can penetrate it. The result is the polyspermy block, protecting the oocyte from fertilisation by more than one sperm.

questions.learning_objective: State that the zona reaction blocks further sperm from entering the egg.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.14 row 29 = e; stem confirmed by direct render (page 6)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Day the morula reaches the uterine cavity
questions.question: On what day does the morula reach the uterine cavity after fertilization?

explanations.A: Correct. After fertilisation in the ampulla, tubal cilia and muscular contractions carry the dividing conceptus along the uterine tube. By about the 4th day it has reached the 16-cell morula stage. At that point it enters the uterine cavity, where it continues developing into a blastocyst over the following day or two.
explanations.B: Incorrect. By the 7th day, the conceptus has already progressed well beyond the morula -- implantation itself is beginning around this time, not tubal transport.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The 9th day is well into the implantation window, not the timing of the morula's arrival in the uterine cavity, which happens several days earlier.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The 8th day, like the 7th and 9th, falls within the implantation window, too late for the morula's arrival in the uterine cavity.
explanations.E: Incorrect. By the 10th day implantation is essentially complete or nearly so -- far later than the morula's arrival in the uterine cavity.

questions.learning_objective: State that the morula reaches the uterine cavity by about the 4th day after fertilisation.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.14 row 30 = a
